title: Painting the Moment
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · How history paintings make a myth

hero.credit: Emanuel Leutze, *Washington Crossing the Delaware*, 1851. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Public domain.

objective: Students will read the two paintings the exhibition’s posters are built around, Trumbull’s *Declaration of Independence* and Leutze’s *Washington Crossing the Delaware*, as **history paintings**: scenes composed long after the event, with a focal point, a structure and a mood chosen by the painter. They will see how those choices help make the story people remember, then plan and sketch a scene of their own from the exhibition.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Most people’s picture of 1776 comes from paintings made long afterward. An artist who can read those choices can see the myth, and make images of their own on purpose.

materials: Both paintings projected, from the two posters; the *Show your class* page (page 3)
Pencils, paper for thumbnails, colored pencils if you have them; differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** on each poster, the painting rises in details beside the text: Trumbull’s delegates, the draft on the table and Hancock in his red chair; Leutze’s rowers, the ice, and Washington with the flag behind him. Have students find each detail and say what it adds to the paragraph beside it.

steps.title: Where does your eye go?
script: Project Leutze’s painting for a full minute in silence. Then ask: *“Where does your eye go first? How did the painter make it go there?”* Most eyes land on Washington, standing against the brightest part of the sky, or on the flag. Ask about the mood. Then give one fact: Leutze painted it in **1851**, seventy-five years after 1776. *“He never saw this moment. Everything here is a choice.”*

steps.purpose: Look before knowing: let the painting work on students, then ask how.
students: Where does your eye go first? How did the painter make it go there?
What mood does the painter want you to feel?

steps.title: Two history paintings
script: Show both paintings (page 3) and read them with the five questions. **Trumbull** builds a calm, wide room: the delegates in rows on both sides, the light falling on the floor and on the five men at the center, the strongest red in the curtains and in Hancock’s armchair. **Leutze** builds a strong diagonal: the boat runs across the canvas, oars and poles cut against it, and Washington stands highest, against the brightest sky.
Compare the moods: order and ceremony against danger and effort. Ask which painting feels more like the beginning of a nation, and why.

steps.purpose: Read both paintings with the same questions, side by side.
students: Find the focal point of each.
One is calm, one is in motion. How does each painter do it?

steps.title: What is left out
script: Then read what the exhibition says beside them. Trumbull’s painting shows the draft being presented; most delegates signed the parchment on August 2, and George Washington never signed at all: he was commanding the army. Ask: *who is not in this room, and what happened before and after?* A history painting chooses one moment and makes it the story.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels read the same two paintings and end with a thumbnail sketch of a moment from the exhibition.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Find the focal point, the brightest light and the diagonal in Leutze’s painting with a checklist, then sketch a moment from the posters with one focal point and one light source.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare Trumbull and Leutze in a chart of five questions, then plan a scene in two thumbnails and write a short artist’s statement.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Judge how each painting helps make the myth the poster describes, including the flag in Leutze’s boat, then design a scene that tells the story more truly and defend your choices.

steps.purpose: Read the paintings closely, then compose a scene, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read the same two paintings and end with a scene of your own.

steps.title: A gallery of moments
script: Lay the sketches out as a quick gallery. Three students, one from each level if you can, point to their focal point and name one thing they left out on purpose. Ask the class: *which sketch would change how people picture 1776?*

screen.text:
Most people picture the Declaration from paintings made decades later.
What will your picture make people remember?

steps.purpose: Share the sketches and name the choices in them.
students: What did you leave out, and why?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
